title: What it takes to restore a fjord
content: Kaare Manniche Ebert stands on a wooden jetty, scanning the water for clumps of eelgrass. Then he wades in, gently sweeps his fishing net past one growing on the sandy bottom, and pulls out two little grey shrimp and a few shellfish. “Life has come back, but it's still not convincing,” he says. Ebert is a fish biologist and has been an adviser to the Danish Sports Fishing Association for about 30 years. Over the decades, he has watched life slowly disappear from Vejle Fjord. Situated on Denmark's Jutland peninsula, about a three-hour drive west of Copenhagen, the fjord has become a focal point in the debate over nitrogen pollution in Denmark – and across Europe. “Just 15 years ago, sea trout used to stay here the entire year because there was a lot of food for them. There used to be big sand worms swimming around in the water,” Ebert recalls. This year, he has only fished in the fjord twice. “To catch a sea trout, I have to fish for about ten hours. That's a lot of work for one fish.” Two years ago, Ebert says, he couldn't find any life among the eelgrass. Shrimp and various species of small fish are now present again. title: Europe's loneliest reaches
content: Sometimes you just want to be left alone. But where would you go? We scoured the map to find the places you are least likely to bump into other humans – the spots furthest from any road. We discovered that in most European countries, you're never more than 10 kilometres from the nearest road. But at the heart of Iceland's Vatnajökull glacier lies Europe's most remote location, which would require a trek of at least 46 kilometres to reach. Draw a perfect circle around this point and you get an area of almost 7,000 square kilometres – more than four times the size of London – that is largely devoid of people.

title: Sell staff data, give it to a bot, fire staff, hire bot
content: If you had to put a price on your job, what would it be? I’m not talking about your salary, but the true value of what you do every day. Not sure? Google might have an idea: it's going to pay USD 10 million for Spirit Airlines' internal business data. The company shut down in May, and the tech giant is going to use employee data from millions of emails, Teams messages, spreadsheets, and calendars to train its AI systems. “Many people are not aware that the way they do their work is valuable because that's what AI is being trained on,” Wouter Zwysen, senior researcher at the European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), told The European Correspondent. European labour agreements are starting to include rules on the use of AI to assist or monitor employees. But they don't often cover the economic gains that employers are making from selling workers’ knowledge as data, a recent study co-edited by Zwysen shows. It analyses more than 170 collective agreements in eight EU countries and finds that while most industries show a lack of understanding about the value of that data, the creative sector stands out as an exception. title: The dentist won't be seeing you now
content: Got a toothache? Tough luck. Across much of Europe, dental care comes out of your own pocket. Around 10 million people in the EU skipped dental care in 2025, according to Eurostat data, mostly because of cost. People are four times more likely to skip the dentist where they pay most of the bill. Public healthcare schemes only cover about a third of dental spending in the EU. Germany, France, and Croatia are the exceptions, covering more than 60%. But more money isn't a magic fix. In Denmark, the state’s share of dental spending has held stable at around a third since 2010, yet the share of Danes skipping the dentist because of cost rose from 1.2% to 7.8%. The government now pledges to make dental care free within the next decade. Across 22 countries, more public money for dental care since 2008 didn't mean fewer people skipped the dentist over cost. What could help is making sure that money actually reaches those who need it. In 2025, 5.5% of the EU's poorest adults skipped dental care because of cost, versus less than 1% of the richest. Since 2008, the share of people unable to afford dental care has fallen by 30%. But for many, a trip to the dentist is still a luxury.

title: Pull here to slow the climate crisis
content: Methane is a greenhouse gas responsible for roughly a third of today’s global heating, and it may be our best chance to curb the climate crisis. Compared to its better-known sibling carbon dioxide (CO₂), which can stay in the atmosphere for hundreds to thousands of years, methane's lifespan is relatively short at only about 12 years. That gives us a solid chance to slow down the climate crisis, according to the European Civil Society Observatory on Methane (CSO-M), and buy time to deal with CO₂ emissions. But where do we start if we want to hit the methane brake? If you imagine the EU's total methane emissions as a pie of three ingredients, one really is burping cows: the majority still come from agriculture. The second ingredient is organic waste, which releases methane as it breaks down in landfills. The third is fossil fuels. Methane can escape to the air in almost any stage of their life cycle, whether released intentionally or leaked by accident. Methane from the energy sector is also the easiest and most cost-effective to reduce, Maria Olczak, senior research fellow at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, told The European Correspondent. title: Dear government, here's some money
content: If I could write a wishlist to the government, it’d be long. Dear government, free public transport for everyone, better education, and more support for cultural projects, please. They’d read it with a smile and a nod, then promptly tell me to give up. How are they supposed to pay for all that? State budgets across Europe are already under pressure. Luckily, I found a solution. Or at least the start of one. European banks are sitting on billions of euros in so-called dormant accounts. When people move abroad, or die without leaving any heirs or telling their heirs about their savings, their bank accounts are often forgotten and left untouched for decades. They become dormant assets – ghost money, if you will. In Germany, estimates for how much money is sitting in dormant accounts range from €4-9 billion. €9 billion! title: Why is it getting so hard to watch football?
content: It's Champions League night. Nine matches are on the schedule. Millions of fans will tune in, some through paid streaming services, others via illegal websites. Either way, watching the beautiful game is getting increasingly complicated. If you've followed the competition for a few years, you probably remember when watching was much simpler. National broadcasters and telecom companies often held football rights and bundled matches into their TV, internet, and phone packages. That model is changing, said Thomas Peeters, a sports economist and professor at the Erasmus School of Economics. “A lot of the broadcasting rights that used to be free-to-air on one of the channels that you had anyway have been migrating to more streaming services dedicated specifically to sports.” In Germany, for example, DAZN shows all Champions League matches except the top match on Tuesday evenings, which Prime Video holds exclusively. title: In Bulgaria, blood is a family affair
content: “When you pass by the hospital, a man will ask whether you need blood. In 2021, I paid 400 leva (€200) for a unit of blood,” said Hristo (not his real name) from Pernik, Bulgaria. Every day, around 600 Bulgarians need blood donations following accidents, surgeries, or chronic illnesses. Yet under Bulgarian law selling blood is illegal. In 2025, Bulgaria had 182,154 blood donors, according to Pencho Penchev, head of health policy at the Bulgarian Red Cross. That was an increase of about 2.5% from the previous year. Still, only 24 out of every 1,000 citizens donate blood. One reason for the shortfall is Bulgaria's so-called “family model”, under which patients rely on relatives to donate blood. These donations account for 85%-90% of the country's total blood supply. But what happens when you have a rare blood group and none of your relatives can donate? You go outside the hospital, where the dealer – often from the Roma community – offers to pose as a “relative” and donate his blood in exchange for a few hundred euros. “With rare blood types, you have no other choice” continued Hristo. title: Surf's up, borders down
content: The ocean doesn't respect man-made borders, and the Curonian Spit – a 98-kilometre stretch between the coast of Lithuania and Russia's Kaliningrad region – is a perfect example. In the cold Baltic waters, surfers from both countries line up to catch the same waves, but they cannot cross from one side to the other. Between them lies a NATO-Russia border, along which Lithuania’s chief of defence recently suggested installing physical barriers to ensure continuous patrols. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Baltic Sea has become increasingly militarised and a stage for national military exercises. NATO has reinforced its maritime presence with warships, aircraft, and naval drones, while Russia maintains its Baltic Fleet in Kaliningrad. For Dima, surfer and member of Nida Surf Club on the Lithuanian side, nature makes these divisions look absurd. Both countries have the “same wind, same waves, same nature,” he tells The European Correspondent. title: Field notes from a failed COP31
content: Friday evening, the official final day of the COP31 climate negotiations. Standing on a chair with a red noose around his neck, Malaysian activist Amalen Sathananthar shouts: “You are killing the future! Why don’t you just kill me now?” It took two additional days – almost 50 hours into overtime – for delegates to give up. The EU and others rejected the final draft because it left out the two words at the root of the climate crisis: fossil fuels. They disappeared under pressure from Saudi Arabia and the Arab Group, backed by a bloc of like-minded developing countries, opposed to any mention of fossil fuels or “top-down” targets. The text “does not begin to address the climate emergency we face,” said Irish minister Darragh O'Brien. “The EU cannot accept it.” His words were met with applause. What is now the longest COP on record, is the first since 2009 to end without an overarching agreement. But this may not be the worst possible outcome. “This collapse is better than a half-hearted final document would have been,” said Johan Rockstrom and Ottmar Edenhofer from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. title: Your boss may not be ready to manage AI
content: If you have an office job, chances are you’ve had at least one earnest chat about how AI could streamline your work. Across Europe, 67% of companies are already using generative AI tools, while another 13% plan to do so in the next year. In a 2025 survey more than 70% of Europeans said they felt AI could improve their productivity, while at the same time overwhelmingly supporting safeguards to ensure its responsible use in the workplace. “You can have good principles, but who is responsible for implementing them inside companies?” asked Maxime Legrand, president of the European managers trade union association CEC. “In practice, that’s managers.” Yet much is still unknown about how AI is actually being used in the workplace. That's why his organisation is collaborating with the Technical University of Munich on a study examining how companies are adopting and managing the technology. title: Working for nothing
content: How would you feel if I told you that, from today, you would no longer be paid for your work until the end of the year? For millions of women, this is effectively what the gender pay gap amounts to. Every year, the French feminist movement Les Glorieuses turns the gender pay gap into a date marking when women in effect start working for free. This year, the campaign celebrates its 10th anniversary. In France, that moment fell on 19 November at 10.51 – hence its #19Novembre10h51 movement. But what if we applied the same calculation across the EU? According to Eurostat, women in the EU earned, on average, 11.1% less per hour than men in 2024. Applying Les Glorieuses’ methodology, this translates into approximately 28 unpaid working days. On that basis, the EU's symbolic date would fall on 23 November 09.12. But why does the gender pay gap persist? Among other reasons, women remain overrepresented in lower-paid sectors, take on a greater share of unpaid care work – which can lead to more part-time employment – and have fewer opportunities to progress into senior roles. title: Taking down the old Serbia
content: For as long as I can remember, Vojislav Šešelj's face has looked down over Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city. A giant poster of his head stood on one of the city’s central boulevards, despite years of protests and complaints. Šešelj leads the far-right Serbian Radical Party, and the UN war crimes tribunal in The Hague convicted him of crimes against humanity in 2018. He was also a long-standing political ally of Vučić's ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), and a prominent figure on the Serbian nationalist right since the 1990s. The poster carried a message denying the Srebrenica genocide. Despite an inspection ordering its removal last year, it remained in place. On the night of 25 October, as citizens celebrated the Student List's historic election victory over Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling SNS party, they took the poster down themselves. Scenes like the one in Novi Sad have become the new normal in Serbia. title: How much are our great-great-great-great-grandkids worth?
content: The year is 3026. One of your descendants, roughly 30 generations down the line, is heading to work. Maybe they live in a solarpunk paradise of green rooftops and take a fully electric bus. Or maybe they wake up in a sealed habitat and check the day's toxicity rating before strapping on an oxygen mask for the short walk to the underground commute, where they're safe from wildfire smoke and unpredictable storms raging above. You’ll never meet them, and after so many generations, they likely won’t even carry your DNA. But they will have inherited something from you: up to 40% of the carbon dioxide emitted today will still be in the atmosphere when they’re born. That carbon will shape the world they live in. So how do we account for the damage it will do to them? One way is to make emitting carbon cost money, which discourages pollution and raises funds for cleaner alternatives. It’s the idea behind a familiar climate slogan: “Make polluters pay.” And the bill for not cutting emissions is already here: the floods that hit the Iberian Peninsula at the beginning of the year, for example, cost €7 billion in relief payments alone. title: Life's cheaper in the east
content: A few weeks ago, I had a train to catch from an Ostbahnhof – the East Station – of a large German city. The area around it felt rougher than the neighbourhoods next to it: a few loveless shopfronts, run-down streets. It wasn’t the first time I’d noticed this at an Ostbahnhof, and it left me wondering. Are the eastern sides of cities generally worse off? There may be something to it. Some cities such as London and Paris have known east-west divides, and researchers studying English cities have found that some of these divides are, in part, a legacy of industrial air pollution. In the late 19th century, the prevailing winds carried factory smoke eastwards. Those who could afford it settled in the cleaner west, and the east stayed poorer. Long after the factories closed, rents there are still cheaper. But the pattern doesn’t hold everywhere. In Brussels, the east is the wealthier side. And in Berlin, the poorer east probably owes more to a different historical divide, the city’s split during the Cold War.

title: The last good meal before the front
content: A warm bowl of borscht in a cold country, after a long day of work. Maybe that's what happiness is all about. I'm sitting in Trypichchia, a traditional restaurant in Kharkiv, a city about 30 km from Russian positions. And this borscht, I swear to god, might be the best I've ever had in my entire life. As a devoted enthusiast, I've eaten it in every possible setting: in fancy restaurants, at petrol stations, in village canteens, in shelters, and in trenches. I know my borscht. Mykyta, 29, one of the founders, tells us that the place started out as a local canteen at the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion. Its sole purpose was to feed soldiers and volunteers who had stayed in the city when Russian forces were on the verge of capturing it. title: Here, have some cancer with your smoky bacon crisps
content: The taste of smoke triggers memories of cosy firesides and tasty barbecues. Think smoked ham, smoked salmon, smoked cheese, and the less traditional smoky bacon crisps. Smoke flavourings are usually made by burning wood, capturing the smoke, and turning it into a liquid that can be added to food. But these smoky flavours may damage DNA and risk causing cancer, EU food experts said in 2023, leading to an EU ban on eight substances that came into effect in July for flavours added to sauces, soups, and snacks. And more are now set to be snuffed out: a wider ban on smoke flavourings in ham, fish, and cheese will land in 2029. The traditional method of exposing food to smoke and heat in a smokehouse oven, though it too can introduce some toxic compounds, is still allowed. The flavourings industry has tried, and failed, to fight back. Food flavourings companies Kerry Inc and Kerry Ingredients last week lost their legal fight to overturn the ban for three flavours they make. title: Grand Theft Wage
content: Grand Theft Auto VI came out on 19 November. It's the most anticipated video game of the decade (the last GTA came out in 2013), reportedly one of the most expensive ever made, and potentially one of the most profitable. Some predictions suggest it could bring in up to USD 5 billion in global sales in its first week alone. Europe is a massive market for GTA. The game costs around €80 in most countries, but its affordability varies once you factor in purchasing power. A familiar pattern in globalised products, like a Netflix subscription. For both, Ukrainians get the worst deal. The hype over the past few days has been insane. Gaming is a world of its own, but GTA is one of those rare franchises that breaks out of that bubble and gets everyone talking, including the mainstream media. Some viral headlines have even warned of a productivity drop as employees call in sick to play, something dubbed “GTA Flu”. But as The Guardian points out, GTA Flu seems to be more of a media phenomenon than an actual economic crisis. Still, the fact that we're even talking about it says something about the scale of this cultural moment.

title: The trouble with pet turtles and pink flowers
content: If you went on a walk this summer, you might not have noticed anything out of place. Pink flowers blooming near the riverbank. A turtle with a red stripe behind its eye sunbathing on a log. A raccoon enjoying its breakfast next to your rubbish bin. But the Himalayan balsam, pond slider, and raccoon that you might have seen are all on an EU list of species it considers a major threat to native ones. The list of “invasive alien species of Union concern” currently includes 114 plant and animal species that were introduced accidentally or deliberately into a natural environment where they are not normally found. EU countries are required to try to prevent accidental introductions, catch and eradicate new arrivals quickly, and manage the species that have already become widespread. A TEC analysis of the geographical spread of 75 invasive alien species of Union concern shows that 83% are present in more than one country, and 60% are reported in at least five. The success of invasive alien species can be attributed to a couple of important shared characteristics, according to Piero Genovesi, biologist and chair of the IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group. title: No olives left to pick
content: It's olive harvest time in Italy, but in many parts of Puglia, there's nothing left to pick. Since 2013, the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa has killed at least 20 million olive trees in Salento alone. The bacterium chokes the tree’s water supply until it dries out. In areas near the outbreak, every host plant within 50 metres of a new case must be felled to prevent the disease spreading. An estimated 33,000 jobs have been lost in Puglia, according to the farmers’ association Confagricoltura. “This is the most serious agronomic problem in the EU,” said Patrizio Ziggiotti, secretary general of the Puglia-based charity Save The Olives, which was set up to confront the crisis and help farmers. The bacterium is thought to have arrived on ornamental plants from Central America, and has since been detected in Spain, France, and Portugal. Olives are central to southern European history and culture. In Greek mythology, Athena won the patronage of Athens by giving the city an olive tree. title: The information war in your comments
content: “Spamouflage” is an operation you may never have heard of. It best embodies a phenomenon we likely all interact with on a daily basis on social media: coordinated state-backed attempts to manipulate online conversations. In 2023, Meta took down 7,704 Facebook accounts and 954 Pages belonging to Spamouflage, a Chinese bot network it linked to Chinese law enforcement. Hundreds of accounts posted comments on Facebook written to sound “personal” and aimed at Western governments, voters, and critics of Beijing. One bot wrote that the 6 January attack on the US Capitol “made the world see the hypocrisy and unbearable [sic] of ‘American democracy,'” according to influence operation tracker Graphika. Fake commenters often adopt invented identities. “Sometimes the bots are even given a bit of personality, like ‘I'm a Black American’ or ‘I'm a doctor in the Midwest,’” Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, told TEC. Spamouflage accounts replying to news outlets and public figures typically criticise or harass them. Some pose as members of groups tied to those they are attacking, Graphika analyst Lili Turner told TEC. AI makes these tactics easier to deploy.

title: The electric truck is ready. Europe is not
content: Your latest online delivery probably travelled to you by road, and so does a quarter of all other goods delivered in the EU. The final stretch is usually covered by small vans, many of them electric, but heavy trucks were also likely involved in connecting manufacturers and smaller couriers. And those are still mainly powered by diesel engines. By 2030, an EU law requires heavy-duty truck and bus manufacturers to cut the carbon emissions of the vehicles they produce by 45% compared to 2019. According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), that means at least a third of all new trucks currently bought in the EU need to be zero-emission, mainly electric. Now, fewer than 3% are. For manufacturers, shifting production to e-trucks only makes sense if there's demand. “Obviously, you don't produce these vehicles without having someone who wants to buy them,” Thomas Fabian from ACEA told The European Correspondent. And why aren't people buying? Lack of charging infrastructure, mainly. title: The EU sidelines its top diplomat
content: The EU has a top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, to jet around the world meeting with global leaders on behalf of its 27 member states. She's the international face of the EU, meant to represent all EU citizens and their interests in the world. Except when she isn't. Last week, EU governments picked five countries for potential negotiations with Russia to discuss ways to end its war against Ukraine: France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and one non-EU member, the United Kingdom. These are known as the E5 group of “Europe's five leading military powers”. Also on the list: EU representatives from the European Commission and the European Council, which organises meetings of EU leaders. Wait, back up a bit, there are talks with Russia? Sort of. title: Searching for a good day for honey
content: On a perfect summer's day in Latvia, there’s barely any wind and the flowers are producing nectar. “20 degrees and up, with sunshine – that’s an ideal day,” says Valters Brusbārdis, who kept bees for 30 years before selling them all last spring. He also chairs the Latvian Beekeepers’ Association. June and July are usually the most reliable months for making honey, he said. For a professional beekeeper in Latvia, more than 50kg of honey per colony makes a good season. Some of his fellow beekeepers told him they’d had record harvests this year. In 2023, Eurostat counted a record 9.4 million hives on EU farms, 16% more than in 2020. Italy had the highest number, followed by Romania, and Greece. But the figures exclude wild bees, and tell us nothing about the health of the bees living in these hives. Bees and the climate In Bulgaria’s Pirin Mountains, beekeeper Ivan Geshev has seen the effects of the climate crisis on his bees since 2016, from droughts to sharp temperature swings. He estimates that his summer worker bees now live five or six days less than they used to, leaving fewer bees to collect pollen and nectar. title: The antidote to TikTok tourism? A free paper map
content: Planning a city trip in Europe? Chances are you’ll scroll TikTok for ideas or ask ChatGPT to build an itinerary. But have you considered using a paper map instead? Sound old-school? It might be what you actually need. Meet USE-IT Europe, a network of free city maps made by young locals who want to share with visitors where they actually spend their time. The maps cover the usual ground – where to eat, drink, shop, relax – but each one also comes with a five-minute history of the city and an “Act like a local” section full of dos and don’ts. In Prague for example, don’t order the chimney cake. It’s “not Czech, not traditional, and not so good.” Depending on the city, you might also find Spotify playlists, useful local phrases, and suggestions on what to order at a bar or bring to a picnic in the park. The maps are full of practical tips too, from free concerts to places where you can get free tap water. “Honest tourist information from locals for young travellers. content: Nine robots dance clumsily on the stage of Lisbon's FIL Arena. “This is our time, this is our fight” go the lyrics of the song. “This was the biggest robot dance performance outside of China!” the event's moderator proclaims. title: The grand art-taking - Tracking Europe's missing paintings
content: Over the past century, art thieves have stolen 27 Van Gogh masterpieces across Europe, more than any other famous artist by a healthy margin. But if you add up mainstream cinema hits, TV series, and even docu-dramas, the favourite victim is Rembrandt, followed by Degas and Rubens. Van Gogh’s lead owes a lot to one very ambitious night. On 14 April 1991, 20 paintings vanished from Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum. Two armed men had hidden inside the building and, as it turned out, had help from within. Yet the world-famous Dutch painter remains underrepresented on screen, appearing in just two action films: The Train and the less-known Righteous Thieves, both involving Nazi art plundered during World War II. As for locations, both real-life and fictional art theft love glamorous capitals like Paris and London. Where the film industry exaggerates is the method: forged copies, disguises, and acrobatic roof-suspension instead of nighttime break-ins and improvised ladders. title: Berlin's big plan to evict its landlords
content: Tobi lives in a 50 sq metre apartment in Berlin-Neukölln. His landlord, the real estate company Deutsche Wohnen, thinks it has a storage room. It does not. Every two years, Deutsche Wohnen sends Tobi a letter announcing a rent increase, listing the storage room as a feature that has not yet been priced into his rent. Each time, Tobi refuses. “I respond that no, I still don’t have a storage room. Or they tell me that my bathroom tiles, which are plain white except for two small lines of red and orange square tiles, are a value-adding feature. title: Locked up and handed a pill
content: “Can you imagine being locked in one place from morning to night?” Federico Mollo, 51, told The European Correspondent. He spent eight years in Italian prisons between 2011 and 2019 for a homicide conviction. From prison, he completed a high school diploma, worked, took writing classes, and joined the prison's band. “I did everything I could,” he said. “Being locked in a cage makes you lose your mind.” About one third of European prisoners suffer from mental health disorders, according to a 2021 survey by the World Health Organization (WHO). title: Who keeps cooking Europe’s frozen peas?
content: In the early hours of 12 October, a delivery driver pulled up to a French supermarket to find its cold-storage room flooded, with temperatures set to a balmy 50°C. That night, over 700 stores were hacked across the country, and millions of euros' worth of food wasted. Three weeks later, similar attacks targeted retailers in 16 European countries. In France, three blood banks narrowly prevented another disaster thanks to early alarms and intervention systems. Who's coming for our fridges? European and national authorities are struggling to figure out who's behind these attacks, and available evidence is highly disputed. Cybersecurity sources consulted by The European Correspondent said they believe state actors to be the most likely culprits. title: Relax, the embassy of Finland in Canberra is open again
content: Here's something I never thought I'd write: the embassy of Finland in Australia has gone viral. It all started when the Finnish embassy in Canberra announced it would be closed on Tuesday, 10 November, for “an internal planning day” (which turned out to be an end-of-the-year sauna day for the team). Nobody knows why, but the internet lost its mind. Thousands of people all across the world started posting memes on social media about how devastated they were, or how the closure had ruined their day. Like this video with more than 11 million views, or this one joking that riots in Paris were sparked by news of the closure. If you're not familiar with meme culture, the joke is that there is no joke. Nobody actually cares that a small embassy in Canberra is closed for a day (no offence to the staff). The fun is in everyone pretending it's a global catastrophe. But why this particular embassy, and why now? One theory is that the embassy's account was already gaining more attention after a post promoting an all-expenses-paid trip to Finland for 16 singles from across the world, “complete with dinner dates with local Finns” and organised by Finland's national tourism organisation.

title: Europe's invaders have red claws
content: Lake Milada, one of Czechia's largest lakes, is home to a diverse range of animals: European catfish, greylag geese, and smooth snakes. But in September, recreational cyclists came across an unusual sight: a red crayfish marching on the path. While crayfish are not new to the country – signal and spiny-cheek crayfish have displaced native species over the years – this one was different. It was a red swamp crayfish, which is found in freshwater in about 20 European countries, but had never been spotted in Czechia before. Originally from North America, these crayfish are among the most invasive in Europe. For nature conservationist Lenka Čolobentičová and her colleagues at the country's Nature Conservation Agency, it was not good news. “They’re very aggressive; they fight a lot with other crayfish species, they carry the crayfish plague, and they reproduce quickly,” she told The European Correspondent. title: The EU wants to make the internet less shitty
content: “It needs to be nice at first. But then make it shitty,” says the “enshittificator” in a Norwegian Consumer Council video, who explains how companies offering digital services have made the internet less user-friendly. It's satire of “enshittification”, a concept coined by author Cory Doctorow to describe how much of the internet has got less useful or even worse over the years. It taps into growing frustration with online services that use “dark patterns” to nudge people to buy things they may not want, along with addictive design to keep us scrolling. Think of prices you can't find on a website, subscriptions that are incredibly hard to cancel, or warnings that a product is running out so you need to buy it now. Can we clean this up? The European Commission thinks it can, by cracking down on some of these manipulative features. It wants to ban dark patterns and require companies to tell us how to switch off addictive features that encourage compulsive or excessive use. title: Belgium's own ICE could be the first of many in Europe
content: Only 16% of third-country nationals (people not from the EU or EEA) who were ordered to leave Belgium in 2025 actually did so. To raise that number, the Belgian parliament passed the “home raids law” last week. It allows police officers, with authorisation from a judge, to enter private homes and arrest foreign nationals who have refused an order to leave the country and are considered a risk to “public order” or “national security”. In protest against the new measure, 3,000 people formed a human chain around the Palace of Justice in Brussels and demonstrations took place in some 60 municipalities. title: Türkiye is leading climate talks while burning coal
content: COP31 host, Türkiye, is one of the world's 10 largest coal consumers. One of the main themes of the COP31 action agenda is electrification: replacing fossil fuels with electricity in sectors such as transport and industry. But electrification only cuts emissions if the electricity itself is clean, and in Türkiye coal is still the main source of electricity. Türkiye has pledged to speed up electrification, with a proposed national target of raising electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. Climate and energy campaigner at Greenpeace Türkiye, Emel Türker Alpay, told TEC the country's coal strategy is a short-sighted way of pursuing energy independence. It's also costly: the government provides around €2.4 billion a year in subsidies and incentives to support coal, aiming to boost domestic output, reduce dependence on energy imports, and protect jobs in coal-producing regions. And because some of that coal is imported, she argued, it does little to make Türkiye energy-independent. And the cost of dependence is rising. title: Europe just can't kick its cookie habit
content: How long do you think people usually spend on a webpage before clicking? If you guessed 41 seconds or less, you get a cookie. Or, well, a couple of dozen. A disproportionate amount of our time online is eaten up dealing with cookie banners. Depending on how it's measured, each interaction takes between five and 23 seconds. In a national survey, 82% of Germans said they found cookie banners annoying. A separate European poll found 39% of users quickly accept cookies just to get rid of them. That may be no coincidence. Experts have long warned that the advertising industry deliberately designs cookie banners to make them difficult to navigate, nudging you into sharing more of your data. And even when we manage to refuse, a study found that up to 65.4% of websites may still collect our data. But cookie banners aren't inevitable. A growing movement is calling for an alternative: setting your preferences once in your browser which would then communicate these choices to websites. The EU has been considering this approach for years. But efforts to introduce it have repeatedly failed during negotiations. In October, a vote by the Council of the EU killed it again, possibly for good. Why?

title: There's a health app for that. Or is there?
content: A friend recently suggested I get a mole on my back checked, just to be safe. As I'm pretty doctor-avoidant (possibly partly a Dutch cultural thing), I remembered the emails my health insurer had been sending me with subject lines like “Check your skin using this smart skin-check app”. I downloaded SkinVision for “unlimited scanning”, fully reimbursed by my insurer. The app promised to tell me “within 30 seconds” whether my mole was dangerous. Once I'd managed to reach the spot with my phone, it delivered its verdict: “low risk”. Great news! An app covered by my health insurer and used by millions of people must be trustworthy, right? Unfortunately, not quite. Earlier this year, researchers at Ghent University and its university hospital published a study assessing SkinVision's accuracy and the university issued a warning. According to the study, the app was wrong in 15% of analyses. It sometimes flagged harmless moles as dangerous and, worse, missed one in four skin cancers. “As a result, many dermatologists are being flooded with harmless moles,” said Niels Chavannes, professor of family medicine at Leiden University who tests health apps for the Dutch National eHealth Living

title: Europe's anti-abortion movement is rich and powerful
content: Six years after Poland's constitutional court imposed a near-total abortion ban on 22 October 2020, thousands of people took to the streets in Warsaw and over 20 other cities. “Women’s hell continues”, read one placard. Abortion is now legal in Poland only in cases of rape, incest, or when a pregnancy poses a threat to the woman's life or health, forcing many women to terminate their pregnancies secretly, or abroad. Today, protesters blame prime minister Donald Tusk’s government for failing to keep its promise to liberalise abortion laws after winning the 2023 election. Although parliament passed two bills in October to ease restrictions – described by activists as “breadcrumbs” – conservative President Karol Nawrocki is expected to veto them. Despite being home to one of the most restrictive abortion laws in Europe, Poland is not the only place where anti-abortion movements are putting reproductive rights at risk. A report by the Centre for Reproductive Rights found that over the past decade, Europe has seen an overall positive trend towards reforms improving access to abortion care. However, in some countries, outdated legal and policy barriers continue to block or delay access.

title: The strange appeal of Spain's useless bar napkins
content: Anyone who's been to Spain will recognise the little white napkins and dispensers found in its bars and restaurants. Try wiping your greasy fingers after eating a jamón croqueta or cleaning up a spilled caña, and you'll quickly discover they're pretty useless. You can easily get through half a dozen and still end up with dirty hands. These flimsy little things, known as servilletas, are an icon of traditional Spanish bar culture. In some places, a floor covered in them is apparently a good sign: it means the place is popular (although the habit has become less common as local authorities have cracked down on littering). But if they're so useless, why do Spanish bars keep using them? I decided to find out. Turns out I've been using them wrong all along. Servilletas are made from sulfite paper. It's not particularly absorbent, but it does resist grease. And that's the whole point. “They're useful because they really are a good barrier against liquids and sauces you can find in saucy sandwiches or saucy tapas,” Alberto García Moyano explained to me. title: Ever dreamt of living in a castle?
content: The housing market has been bad for so long that I am ready to expand my horizons. But rather than turning to the usual suspects, like tiny homes or van life, I'm dreaming big: castles! Turns out there's more to them than I thought. Castles were originally built as fortified dwellings. Fancy homes for royalty and nobility without defensive fortifications are called palaces. And what about fortresses? Think castles built mostly for stationing soldiers – like knights. Of course, we shouldn't forget ruins, which for our purposes are rather uninhabitable. So far, my quest has led me to two insights. Castles dominate western Europe, while palaces are more common in the centre of the continent, and fortresses tend to cluster around historical frontiers. But, more importantly, with the state of natural gas prices, heating a castle would be a nightmare – and I hate being cold.

title: What it takes to get Europe on a bike
content: On 22 September in Turin, Italy, a car driver hit and killed a seven-year-old boy cycling to school. “That could have been me, or my daughter, or anyone, really. Because that place is dangerous,” resident Maria Cristina Caimotto told us. Every morning since then, Caimotto has joined a crowd of people on bikes in the street where the tragedy took place to show solidarity with the family, but also to ask for safer streets and fewer cars. “We cannot erase what happened. We can only do everything we can so that it does not happen again,” she said. Backed by 13 civil society associations, the activists want Turin to move away from its dependence on cars. It’s ambitious, but not impossible: a similar tragedy helped push the Netherlands to become the cycling country it is today. Until the 1970s, the Netherlands was full of cars. title: Gay sheep don't come cheap
content: “That one flehmened. He wants sex,” farmer Michael Stücke says, pointing to a ram (a male sheep) tilting its head up and curling its upper lip back. This way of smelling the air is known as the flehmen response, which male animals often do before mating. We’re standing in a pasture on Stücke’s sheep farm in the German town of Löhne in North Rhine-Westphalia, observing what looks like a regular flock of sheep. In reality, it may be the world’s most famous: 36 sheep, but they’re all rams, and they’re all gay. Rams that show no interest in mating with ewes (female sheep) and instead pursue other rams are relatively useless to breeders, Stücke says, so they’re usually sent to slaughter. That is, until 2023, when advertising agency Serviceplan started buying them up at auctions and giving them a permanent home on Stücke’s farm, himself a gay farmer. A friend of his working at the agency was sad to hear about what happens to gay rams, and knew he was active in an association for gay farmers. title: Your family's social status still determines yours
content: France, Germany, Portugal, the Netherlands, Italy, and beyond. Young people were once again on the streets across Europe last Saturday. These protests had different triggers, for instance anger over school conditions in France, or opposition to the potential return of conscription in Germany. But there's one shared, underlying frustration: many young people feel that they won't have a better life than their parents. And there are reasons for that feeling. A decades-long development is coming to a head: social mobility has stalled across much of Europe. It refers to the ability to move up – or down – the social and economic ladder – a core promise of liberal democracy. It's mainly measured by occupation, income, and education level. Can someone whose parents never went to university get a degree? Can they find a job that pays better than their parents' work does? Increasingly, the answer to both questions is no. In an “average OECD country”, it takes around four to five generations for children from the poorest 10% of households to reach the mean income levels, according to the organisation itself. title: Trains are still safe
content: The recent horrific rail accident in Spain was the second such accident in the country within the past year. Those two crashes have already killed more passengers than in the deadly year of 2013, when 97 passengers died in train accidents, according to Eurostat. The number of major rail accidents and fatalities has generally declined in Europe since 1980 – despite a small uptick in recent years. Trains remain one of the safest modes of transport. As a train passenger, your risk of dying in a rail accident is one third that of a bus or coach passenger and very similar to that of a commercial aircraft passenger. By comparison, car occupants are around 40 times more likely to die than train passengers travelling the same distance.

title: Burning questions about burning trash
content: Depending on where you live, your waste can take several routes. About half of the waste in the EU gets recycled or composted, the rest ends up either in a landfill or a giant furnace. Burning waste in specialised plants can transform that waste into energy – something that Europe constantly needs more of. Sounds like a win-win? Not so fast. Though incinerating waste reduces the amount sent to landfills and the resulting methane emissions, burning generates ashes, metals, and large quantities of CO₂. “Incinerators are among the most carbon-intensive energy sources in some countries,” Janek Vähk, a policy manager at Zero Waste Europe, told us. “Because these plants are less efficient in energy generation, the greenhouse gas emissions per unit of electricity are almost double those of fossil gas power.” Modern waste-to-energy plants, such as Vienna's colourful Spittelau plant, can limit negative environmental impacts with advanced filtering systems. title: What do Taylor Swift and Giorgia Meloni have in common?
content: Taylor Swift, a billionaire pop empress, and Giorgia Meloni, the far-right Italian prime minister, aren't often mentioned in the same breath. But they're caught in a similar battle, both trying to find new ways to fight an army of AI deepfakes by filing for EU trademarks to protect their voices. Swift's company, TAS Rights Management LLC, wants to register her saying “Hey, it's Taylor Swift”, according to a 6 October filing at the EU Intellectual Property Office. Meloni filed on 5 October to register herself saying “Io sono Giorgia Meloni.” While you can't trademark someone's voice as a whole, these trademarks would give them the exclusive right to their voice saying those words. That could technically stop anyone else from using the voice for a deepfake. Infringing a trademark risks lawsuits and claims for financial damage. It might also be easier to get tech platforms to quickly remove trademark-infringing content. Swift already filed for a US trademark for her voice earlier this year. title: Domestic abuse leaves receipts
content: Your bank statement says a lot about your lifestyle. For women, it could also provide early hints of domestic abuse, according to a recent Nature paper. Using data from Lloyds, the UK's largest retail bank, the study found certain banking patterns in domestic abuse victims' statements as early as seven years before they disclosed their situation. The authors compared more than 5,000 women who had told their bank they were experiencing abuse with over 15,600 customers who had not. Women who disclosed abuse were more likely to have missed a payment, and had lower credit scores. They were also more likely to receive welfare benefits, and their savings were £3,500 lower on average. Their spending patterns also differed: they spent less on self-care, such as the dentist, optician, or sports, and more on alcohol – possibly as a coping strategy, the authors noted. They also spent more on taxis and legal fees. They withdrew cash and changed PIN numbers and address more often, which the authors argue could hint at an abuser taking control of their finances, but also victims regaining it after leaving. title: Rioting for a reason
content: If you've glanced at the news lately, you've probably seen many reports about riots, looting, and violence at protests across Europe. These protests are driven mostly by young people demanding better school conditions and affordable housing, among other things. Yet many headlines focus on violence or riots rather than protestors' demands. Of the more than 10,000 news reports of protests in France by European outlets, just 8% of headlines explicitly mentioned protest demands. Meanwhile, around one in three headlines mentioned terms related to violence. In fact, some of the most-used words in headlines are associated with violence, including “riot”, “clash”, “chaos”, and “violence” itself.

title: Why I'm still paying the price of being a mother
content: It’s 9.30. After feeding two sleepy humans aged three and six, getting them ready and walking them to school, I’ve finally sat down at my desk to do some work – paid work I should say – and write this piece I’ve been putting off since the beginning of September. I've been thinking about it ever since I read the report on the motherhood penalty that the Haut Conseil à l’Égalité (HCE), a French national advisory body, published right in the middle of the back-to-school rush, a particularly stressful time of year for a working mother. Until the afternoon school's clubs started less than a month ago, I had to leave my desk every day at 15.30 to pick up the children, while my partner was still at the office. The rest of the day, I'd take them to the park, run their baths, and make dinner. So, yes, motherhood has meant less time to work – and less income. Around a third less than before having children. Sadly, I’m no exception. The same is true of mothers in France, where I come from, in the years following the birth of their first child. title: I took a five-star ride to the front line
content: At the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it was still relatively easy to get to Kramatorsk, a city in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region. I remember my first trip in 2022, by train. I travelled from Kyiv to Kramatorsk on an old Soviet-era train, packed with soldiers and smelling of onions, cold cigarettes, and sweat. Since then, I have used almost every possible way of getting there. By car, bus, Sprinter van, and car rental. But the closer Russian forces moved towards the city, the harder it became to reach. Trains to Kramatorsk stopped running in 2025. Then car-rental companies pulled out of the area, and we could no longer hire cars. “We have trackers on them,” one rental company employee once told me in Kyiv, giving me a threatening look. “Don’t try to fool me.” I took the bus that day. By the end of 2025, getting to Izium, 120 kilometres south of Kharkiv, was still relatively easy. The problem was getting from there to Kramatorsk, another 70 kilometres south. As Russian drones increasingly targeted the road, the vans stopped running. We only discovered this once we were already in Izium, in late October. title: I’m a journalist in Türkiye, but I’m not in jail (yet)
content: In May, I bumped into my colleague Tuğba Tekerek at a gathering of Turkish journalists in Istanbul. “Freelancers should come together and look out for one another,” she said. “Sure,” I told her. “Let's brainstorm soon.” We never got the chance. Tuğba and I both worked at Deutsche Welle Turkish, although at different times. In 2024, she traveled to Georgia to report for a range of outlets, including LGBTI+ rights association Kaos GL. She's now in jail because of that reporting. When I started out as a journalist in 2010, losing a job didn't necessarily mean the end of a career. A colleague who was laid off could usually find another position. Today, stories like Tuğba's are becoming all too common. Türkiye is due to hold its next scheduled elections in 2028, unless an early vote is called. As we approach that date, media outlets critical of the governement are increasingly coming under pressure, and being taken over by state-appointed trustees, one by one. title: In the name of the father, the son, and AI
content: The hyperrealistic image on the wall of the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene in Novolukoml, Belarus, shows a young man in jeans, holding a laptop in one hand and a rosary in the other. It depicts Carlo Acutis, nicknamed the “cyber-apostle” and often described as the first millennial saint. Fittingly, AI helped create it. The image was created by three people: a photographer, a designer, and an AI engineer. It was blessed on 11 October by Archbishop Tadeusz Kondrusiewicz, the former head of the Catholic Church in Belarus. The parish described it as the first such image in the country. But who was Carlo Acutis? Born in London to Italian parents, the teenager became known for promoting Catholicism online, earning him the nickname “God's influencer”. He died of leukaemia in 2006, aged just 15. In 2025, Pope Leo XIV canonised him, making him a saint. Despite all the work involved behind the image, the use of AI as sparked criticism online. title: All Souls or just your cat's?
content: On All Saints' Day (1 November) and All Souls' Day (2 November), millions of Europeans visit cemeteries and light candles in memory of the dead. But few believe the dead can still reach them. While the dead are remembered in this Christian tradition that dates back to the 10th century, few people today believe the dead can still reach out to the living. But what about animals? A Pew Research survey across 10 countries found that people are often more likely to believe that living animals have spirits than to believe the spirits of their dead ancestors can help or harm them. The gap is the biggest in Türkiye, where 81% believe living animals have spirits while 21% think our ancestors can still reach us. In Spain, most people don't believe in either. So don't forget to light a candle for all our furry friends who are still among us!

title: Frontex is eyeing sweeping new powers
content: The EU's border agency Frontex should take charge of deporting migrants, the European Commission said last week. This would put an agency once accused of serious human rights violations at the heart of enforcing new rules to “return” or expel people who haven't been granted the right to stay in the EU. The tougher EU talk on migration follows a harsher stance from right-wing parties who teamed up earlier this year to agree on the Returns Regulation to detain non-EU nationals who have been ordered to leave. They would then be sent to so-called “return hubs”, such as a centre in Albania for people expelled from Italy who can't be deported to an unsafe home country. Frontex currently cooperates with EU governments to remove people from the EU. It worked with them on some 64,000 returns last year, of which 65% were voluntary and 35% forced. It chartered more than 220 flights and reintegrated some 20,000 people back into their home country, which frequently involves paying them to leave Europe. title: Pretty privilege can save lives
content: There’s the yellow swallowtail, a large, bright yellow butterfly with a stunning tail. Then there are less eye-catching species, such as the Alpine grayling – a rather plain-looking, brown butterfly found in the Alps. Recently, more than 21,000 people from over 100 countries took part in a survey rating almost 500 European butterfly species. Their responses were used to create a “beauty index”. Bright colours, particularly yellow and blue, contrasting patterns, and large, serrated wings or tails scored highest. The species that scored highest also had more photos on Flickr and iNaturalist, and more Wikipedia views. They also had more genetic studies and published research. “We had expected this to be the case in terms of public perception,” said Elisabeth Kühn from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ), who coordinated this survey for Germany, in a press release. “However, we were surprised to find the same pattern in scientific research.” It’s not just a butterfly thing. title: Teaching under pressure
content: Teachers love teaching, according to the ones we spoke to in Sweden, Latvia, the UK, Bulgaria, Italy, and Germany. A 2024 European Commission report echoes that, saying nine out of 10 teachers across 23 countries were satisfied with the profession. But many teachers, including our interviewees, are frustrated by government budget cuts, low pay, declining working conditions, and too much paperwork. Only 15% of them feel they are valued by society, according to the Commission report. They're also often striving to hold the attention of children who have grown up with screens or missed some crucial school years during the Covid-19 pandemic. Teenagers' reading scores have fallen sharply since 2012, when smartphones started to become more common. Resentment and anger at how society is failing education – and how education risks failing kids – have fuelled protests and strikes across Europe, especially in France but also in Italy, Spain, Belgium, Greece Portugal, and Ireland. title: Europe is a pumpkin paradise
content: Europe has developed quite an appetite for pumpkins, a crop that isn't native to the continent. More than 1.2 million tonnes were harvested in Europe last year. So how did pumpkins become a Halloween staple? The answer lies in the origins of Halloween, a tradition millions of Scottish and Irish immigrants brought to the United States in the 1800s. They celebrated Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival marking the end of summer and harvest season. To ward off spirits, people hollowed out hard root vegetables like turnips and carved frightening faces into the rind before placing a candle inside. In America, where turnips were scarce, pumpkins offered a convenient alternative. Much easier to carve, they became the defining symbol of Halloween. The tradition has since travelled back across the Atlantic, bringing the pumpkin along with it. Perhaps Europe is taking back Halloween, one pumpkin at a time. Writer’s note: I carved my first pumpkin last weekend, and if that was a struggle, I have no idea how anyone managed to carve a raw turnip without losing a finger.

title: Poland is ditching coal. What happens to its miners?
content: Coal has long been synonymous with Polish energy. Just 20 years ago, 91% of Poland's electricity came from coal. Today, that figure has fallen to around 50%, while wind and solar power account for a quarter of the country's electricity generation. That's a major step forward for a country that started its energy transition from one of the most coal-dependent positions in the EU. Since 2006, Poland’s power-sector emissions have fallen by 30% despite a growing economy and rising electricity demand. That's encouraging news, particularly for southern Poland where some areas have long struggled with poor air quality. One of them is Kraków, my new home. From Kraków – a city that has transformed itself and left much of its smoggy past behind – I travelled north to the Baltic coast, where Poland's energy transition is truly taking off. At the beginning of October, all 76 turbines were installed at Poland's first offshore wind farm. Once fully operational, the wind farm is expected to generate enough electricity to power around 1.5 million homes and meet around 3% of the country's annual electricity demand. content: Having a bad week? Kylian Mbappé might be having a worse one. On Monday, the French football star lost the Ballon d’Or, football's most prestigious individual award, to England's Harry Kane. It all started when a short clip from a French interview, aired six months ago, suddenly went viral at the start of the week. title: Too violent for a war? Perfect for a protest!
content: First, I teared up. Then my nose started itching, and then came the coughs. First from those around me, until I joined the choir myself. The crowd grew uneasy, people looked for a way out, and the chaos began. That's how I experienced tear gas for the first time at a protest in Türkiye in 2025, but it could just as easily describe one of the many protests this month where police used tear gas: be it in Belgium, Italy, Albania, or, most importantly, France. Nowhere has tear gas been used more than in France, the country that gave birth to it. title: Raving, reading, and resisting in Ukraine
content: It could be Berlin or New York. One autumn evening, hundreds gather in the rounded hall of a brutalist building at Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. A DJ plays soft electronic music. Some drink coffee, others sit on the floor with a book. Nobody is dancing. They call it a book rave. Bring a book and read together. Sit with your friends and talk about books. Go to some of the classes and listen to a lecture about literature. Or simply listen to music and meditate. But in Ukraine, books have become more than a pastime. Over the summer, Russian strikes destroyed an estimated 13 million of them. In Kharkiv, a single drone attack burned eight million books at a publisher's warehouse, including school textbooks and children's stories. “Why attack books?” asks Svitlana, one of the book rave's organisers. To her, the destruction recalls the long history of Russian attempts to suppress Ukrainian culture, from imperial language restrictions to Soviet censorship and executions. title: Loans don't grow on trees
content: Ever wondered what tobacco and banks have in common? Very soon, both will be warning consumers about the risks associated with their products. From 20 November, under new EU rules, adverts for consumer credit will have to include a clear and prominent warning: “Caution! Borrowing money costs money.” Very similar to the ones you see on cigarette packets. The requirement to warn consumers that loans don't grow on trees is part of new regulation to protect EU consumers taking out loans. Lenders will also face stricter requirements on the information they provide in credit adverts. This includes the total cost of borrowing and, where applicable, the loan's duration and repayment instalments. Misleading advertising will also be prohibited. The updated rules extend consumer credit protections to small loans of less than €200 and “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) schemes, which have become increasingly common in online shopping. title: How to shut down half a country in 10 days
content: Walking down the aisle of your local supermarket, and all you see are bare shelves and rows of empty boxes. A sign reads: “Delivery not received. Sorry for the inconvenience.” There is no bread, fruit, or vegetables – just frozen food, which you quickly stock up on. This is not a flashback to 2020, when panic-buying for pasta and toilet paper during the Covid-19 pandemic left supermarket shelves emptied. This time, the shortages are linked to workers' protests in southern Italy over soaring fuel prices. It all began with the farmers on 10 October: they called for mass demonstrations in the Italian regions of Calabria, Apulia, Basilicata, and Sicily, and workers in the transport sector immediately joined. Striking hauliers switched off their engines on roads and motorways, and refused to unload their goods. Fishermen also joined the protests, leaving their boats docked at port. The protesters' message is clear: running a farm, a transport or fishing business has become too expensive. Fuel is one major cost, but it's far from being the only one. title: Less friendly with the rest of the world
content: European national football teams play fewer friendlies against non-European opponents than they used to. The number of friendly games played between a UEFA national team and a team from a different confederation dropped from an average of 55.3 games a year before 2019 to 38.6 after 2019. The drop coincides with the launch of the UEFA Nations League in late 2018. This new competition would replace many of the international friendlies teams used to play. UEFA said the aim was to add “status and appeal to national team football.” The number of intercontinental friendlies varies from year to year. It tends to rise in World Cup years, when teams seek opponents from other continents to prepare for the tournament. The number of friendlies rose in 2026, when 43 of the year’s 67 friendlies against non-European teams were played in June, just before the expanded World Cup kicked off.

content: What happened: The Czech right-wing populist government, led by billionaire prime minister Andrej Babiš, wants to fundamentally change the country's public media, trying to abolish the licence fee paid directly by citizens and instead fund Czech TV and radio from the state budget. They fast-tracked the parliamentary debate and scheduled the first round of voting at 4.36 in the morning on Saturday last week. Not exactly a common procedure for voting on something this big. When word spread, spontaneous protest filled the square next to the parliament building throughout the night. The government majority passed the proposal anyway. title: Serbia is free
content: For most of my life, Serbia was a place that you'd better leave. And so I did. But last night, as I followed election results deep into the night all the way from the Netherlands, I felt that Serbia might be a place to come back to for perhaps the first time in my life. Around 21.30 on election night, former president Aleksandar Vučić conceded that his party SNS, which has been in power for the last 14 years, had lost to the Student List, born out of a protest movement that has shaken Serbia since November 2024. Almost instantly, “Serbia is free” echoed all over social media as city streets erupted in joy and celebration. The police, who had been blocking the street in front of the Republic Electoral Commission and patrolling Belgrade since the morning, began to retreat, and two years of building tension was released in fireworks, chants, and dancing deep into the night. The Student List won by a landslide. According to the Republic Electoral Commission, and based on 97% of counted votes, the Student List won 52.65% of the votes and is projected to gain 140 out of 250 parliamentary seats, enough for a parliamentary majority. title: The Black Sea is turning green, and not the good kind
content: “This summer, we went 38 km deep in the Black Sea. You can see how it is more green,” Martin Tomov, a campaigner for Greenpeace Bulgaria, told us. Satellite images from EUMETSAT confirm his observation. The scientific name for this is eutrophication: an excess of nutrients allows algae to bloom, turning rivers and seas from crystal blue to green. It happens when manure or nitrate- and phosphate-based fertilisers spread on farmland run off into rivers. When the algae later die and rot, they strip the water of oxygen, which suffocates fish, and can also release a poisonous gas. “They also block sunlight; it prevents many organisms from surviving, which impacts the entire food chain,” Tomov told us. In 2016, a jogger died on a beach in Brittany, France, after inhaling poisonous gas from rotten algae. A court held the state liable nine years later, and France compensated his family. But Europe is far from responding adequately. Nearly one third of the EU's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters, and 81% of marine waters, are eutrophic according to an EU report from early this year. title: I See You, ICC
content: The International Criminal Court (ICC) won the EU's human rights prize last week, a big vote of support from the European Parliament for its work in putting war criminals on trial and just 13 days after the US imposed sanctions on the tribunal. But it's “somewhat problematic” for the EU's assembly to award the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought to the court “whilst simultaneously being indecisive and arguably weak regarding its responses to the US sanctions,” said Benjamin Thorne, an assistant law professor at the University of Reading. The Hague-based court, backed by 125 countries, has convicted 15 people to date, all from African countries. It currently has arrest warrants for Russian president Vladimir Putin and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. US secretary of state Marco Rubio earlier this month called the ICC a “rogue court” that might prosecute American soldiers, border patrol agents, or elected leaders. title: Man up, don't save the planet
content: Are you a man who cares about the climate? Then you might be a “soy boy” (or for our less chronically online readers: lacking masculine traits). Research suggests that men who want to protect the environment are often seen as warmer and more caring – traits traditionally associated with femininity. Michael Haselhuhn, an associate professor of management at the University of California, published research on this. When asked if they would use cold water for laundry to save money, most men said they would. “When I said it helps the environment because it saves electricity, the support dropped by 10%,” Haselhuhn said. Across most European countries, there is a gender gap in how women and men see environmental issues. Women tend to care more about protecting the environment than men. “In Northern and Western Europe, men are less likely to vote for green parties or parties that emphasise protecting the environment,” said Ingvild Zinober, a researcher studying the green gender gap at the European University Institute. title: Coffeemaxxed lifestyle
content: As a coffee addict, I dream of living in a city where cafés stay open for as much of the day as possible, ideally opening early and closing late. But my past geographical choices haven’t exactly served me well. To find out where I should have settled, I collected Google Maps listings for cafés in about 80 of Europe’s largest cities, covering roughly 15,000 active cafés. The data revealed a few interesting things beyond opening hours. London and Istanbul have the most café listings, but neither scores particularly well in customer reviews. If you’re after the best-rated cafés, Romania is a good choice: Bucharest’s cafés have a median rating of 4.8 out of 5, based on more than 30,000 reviews. Still, Bucharest wouldn’t satisfy me: its cafés stay open for about 10 hours a day. That’s much better than Leeds, where cafés are open for just seven hours on average. For a coffee fanatic like me, the Balkans and Istanbul may be the best bet: cafés in Tirana, Podgorica, Zagreb and Pristina stay open for around 15 hours a day. title: Extremists have no idea what Norse mythology is really about
content: Thor, the Norse god of thunder, once visited the giant Utgard-Loki. The giant challenged him to empty a drinking horn, lift a cat, and wrestle an old woman. He failed all three and left questioning his power. As it turned out, Utgard-Loki had used magic to hide Thor's real opponents. He had been drinking from the ocean, and the cat was Jörmungandr, the gigantic sea serpent encircling the earth. The old lady? Old age itself. This is the Norse myth I remember most clearly. For most people across Scandinavia and Iceland, the old myths don’t play a big role in everyday life, but there are subtle signs of them. Weekdays, streets, and people are named after Norse gods, for instance. Or the countless TV shows, comics, books, and music inspired by old gods and myths. We don't know when and how Norse mythology started, but it was definitely practised in Scandinavia and Iceland in the late Iron Age (from 500 AD) and Viking Age (800-1050 AD). Northern Europe was then gradually Christianised around the year 1000, through missionaries and due to pressure from foreign trade from the south. title: What does the C say about your yoghurt?
content: Let's say you're in a shop looking for yoghurt. You're standing at the fridge, choosing between strawberry and plain. The pots show five letters, running from a dark-green A to a red E. The one you're holding has a C. Hmmm. Those letters are the Nutri-Score, a label weighing sugars, saturated fat, salt, and calories against fibre, protein, and the content of fruit, vegetables and legumes in products per 100 g or 100 ml. The label was first adopted in France in 2017 and has since been picked up in Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and Spain. International supermarkets have also brought it elsewhere, which is why you'll see the label on Lidl shelves in Latvia, for example. Using it is voluntary for producers. title: Your home is their asset
content: Let’s be realistic, housing has always been a business. What has changed however, is its scale. By the end of 2024, the value of global real estate had reached 393 trillion USD (€379 trillion) according to Savills Research real estate analysis. Most of this value came from residential property. This is more than the combined value of all global stocks and debt, and 20 times the value of all the gold ever mined. title: Serbian students are threatening Vučić's long rule
content: When 16 people died after the concrete canopy above the entrance to the train station in Novi Sad (Serbia's second-biggest city) collapsed in November 2024, few could imagine what would follow: two years of mass protests that grew into the largest student protest movement since the fall of Milošević in 2000. title: Giving Amsterdam's streets a face
content: If you live in a European city, it's likely your street is named after someone. But do you know who that person was, what they did to earn a place on the map, or what they looked like? In Amsterdam, finding out might be a little easier. Many streets, squares, and bridges feature information panels with a portrait and a short biography of the historical figure they are named after. And all this thanks to a grassroots initiative run by two Amsterdam residents. Geef straten een gezicht (“Give streets a face”) is a project launched by photographer and graphic designer Paul Fennis in 2013. He installs portraits and short biographies to help people understand the history behind their street names. Since 2020, journalist and writer Shirley Brandeis has worked with him on the project. “It started as a one-off thing,” Brandeis told The European Correspondent. title: Playing by the rules?
content: The strength of courts, rights and checks on power is declining across Europe, reflecting a broader global recession, according to data from the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index. The index measures eight factors, including checks on government power, the absence of corruption and the justice system. Since 2021, Europe's average score has fallen in seven of the eight areas, and remained unchanged in one: corruption. Although the declines are small, less than 1.5 points out of 100, they are consistent. Two-thirds of European countries scored lower in 2026 than in 2021. Russia, Belarus, Türkiye and Serbia remain at the bottom of the European rankings, but some of the steepest declines were also recorded in Georgia, Portugal and Slovakia. Europe still scores substantially higher than the global average, and nine of the world's ten highest-ranked countries are European.

title: How to win (and lose) an ally in 10 days
content: These past few weeks mark a more deliberate and open campaign of coercion against Europe and Ukraine by the US and Russia. Both US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin have something to gain: a better result for the Republicans in the upcoming US midterm elections, a Ukraine pushed into defeat, and a Europe that still depends on the US. What happened: 9 October: Trump and Putin hold a long phone call. Afterwards, the US lifts sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027, letting Russia sell millions of tonnes of it to the US and global markets. Historian Anne Applebaum called it “an abrupt, Hail Mary attempt to force Ukraine to surrender and to save the Russian economy.” Never mind that, according to the EU's economy chief, Russia can't export enough diesel to change prices. On the call, Putin proposes a summit with Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping in China next month to decide Ukraine's future, without Ukraine. According to a Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter, Putin wants a “second Yalta”, the 1945 conference where the US, UK, and Soviet Union carved up Europe, this time with the US, Russia, and China dividing the world between them.

title: Good news, the robots trying to take your job are bad at it
content: A supermarket on the outskirts of Copenhagen has become the unlikely site of a futuristic labour experiment. Føtex is training humanoid robots to restock its shelves at night, a task it estimates currently takes 40-50% of its staff's time. One day, they hope to have two high-tech assistants in every store, not to replace employees but to speed up routine tasks, they say. But for now, the robots aren't exactly autonomous – trainers from the Danish start-up HIVE Robots still guide their every movement using VR goggles. Nor are they... good. Still much slower than humans, they're meant to improve as they accumulate and process data over time. title: Priced out of Netflix
content: When Netflix raised my subscription price again to €17 per month, I paid and moved on. But it made me wonder what the same subscription costs everyone else. I found that Netflix's lower pricing in poorer countries is still far smaller than the gap in wages to richer countries. title: Do we really need all this cheese water?
content: A spoonful of whey in your morning cereal, a protein shake after an intense leg session. For many of us, focusing on protein in our diets has become a habit. Fewer of us know where the protein taking over our supermarkets actually comes from. Gym-goers' favourite product, whey powder, is a by-product of cheesemaking: it starts as the yellowish liquid left over after milk is thickened into curds and strained. That liquid is then dried into powder. Whey keeps most of milk’s lactose and water-soluble vitamins and about a fifth of its protein. For centuries, people drank it (for example the Scottish whey wine called “blaand“) or used it as a medicine for gut health. Today, up to 200 million tonnes of whey are produced as a by-product of industrial cheesemaking globally. The European Union alone makes more than a quarter of it. The hype around high-protein food has increased demand for whey, but production volumes have stayed the same, as they're linked to cheese production. As a result, the price of whey has skyrocketed in Europe in recent months. title: Elected women never asked to be nudified, yet here we are
content: As a person of a marginalised gender, existing online means being constantly amazed by all the ways the internet can be used against you, no matter how powerful you are. One of the latest additions to that arsenal are “nudification” apps, AI-powered tools that can be prompted to create fake, sexually explicit pictures and videos of people, usually without their consent. content: When Portuguese biologist Henrique Pereira was a kid in the 1980s, there were almost no vultures left in southern Europe. title: Your fries are getting shorter (but no less crispy)
content: No matter what the weather did to this year's harvest, Belgium will still deliver its biggest contribution to the culinary cultural canon: fries. They will still taste good. But this season, the long ones may be missing from your paper cone. First came the potato glut. Last year’s harvest was so abundant that potatoes sold without a contract went for between €0 and €5 per 100 kg – far below production costs, said Daniel Ryckmans, an agronomist at the Walloon potato organisation FIWAP.
