title: European businesses are keen to go green
content: The EU has a favourite word: competitiveness. To better compete in the global economy, the European Commission is rewriting (and often weakening) environmental rules for businesses, for example to reduce reporting burdens. Making life easier for our biggest industries sounds reasonable: we shouldn't impose rules that drive them out of business, should we? Yet what do businesses actually want? A recent GlobeScan survey commissioned by the environmental group WWF asked 350 European business leaders. Only 29% said the EU's environmental simplification efforts have helped them, while 55% reported a negative or mixed impact. title: Stamps worth more than your house
content: If you've never thought long and hard about stamps, you are most certainly not a philatelist – a student or collector of postage history. During the stamp craze of the mid-19th century, the French spoke about “timbromanie”, or the mania of rabid philatelist collectors. Who would've thought that humble postage stickers would unleash such heated passion among Europe's well-to-do? The most valuable stamps in the world are mostly the freaks among them, including those printed in the wrong colour or displaying their subject upside down. Others are famous for their lore, like the improvised “1856 British Guiana 1-Cent Magenta” (the second stamp in the visual), printed by British colonists after the Crown failed to send them a new batch in time. As such, stamps have always been as much about power as they are about mail. Colonial and imperial rulers used them to thrust their faces into the daily lives of people; Poland and Czechoslovakia, once independent, reissued stamps from elsewhere by printing right over them.

title: Europeans win, abroad
content: When Belgian physicist Francis Halzen was awarded this year’s Nobel prize in Physics, he became the ninth European among the past 10 physics laureates. But Halzen, who won his prize while working at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, is also part of a less celebrated trend. Four of those nine Europeans carried out the research that earned them the prize outside their home countries, mostly in the United States. The trend runs across all scientific Nobel categories (physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, and economics), where European laureates are increasingly likely to have done their prize-winning work abroad. It is most pronounced in economics, where more than two-thirds of European winners did their Nobel-recognised research at a foreign university. In physics and chemistry, the share is more than a third. The Nobel prize reflects a wider brain drain with European researchers leaving for better-funded positions elsewhere. title: Who owns Albania?
content: Protesters are still waving pink flamingos on wooden poles, over four months into their movement. As they march through the streets in central Albania they chant ”Rama in jail, Berisha in jail,” referring to the prime minister and the opposition leader. Dubbed the Flamingo Revolution, these protests began in opposition to a long-awaited luxury resort linked to Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law. We went to the place that sparked the unrest to understand why the protests show no signs of ending. It's part of a protected area that is home not just to migratory flamingos, but also to Dalmatian pelicans, nesting loggerhead turtles, and the occasional monk seal. title: Want to ditch your gas boiler? Ask your city
content: You may never have worried about the Strait of Hormuz, had it not been for the impact on your wallet, right? With gas prices hitting record highs and fossil fuels contributing to climate change, perhaps it's finally time to say goodbye to the old gas boiler in the bathroom? Hmmm... What seems like an easy choice on paper can be a much harder one in practice. Whether we can make the switch, and when, depends on the alternatives available where we live, how much money we need to invest and whether public support is available to help us go greener. Your local government has a big influence on all three. Local politicians can make practical decisions about heat networks and building renovation. They are also closer to residents, which makes them best equipped to identify people affected by energy poverty and target support where it is needed most. That's precisely what Greenpeace decided to track: they followed 15 European cities and assessed how well they're doing in the green heating race (or whether they are racing backwards). title: Four broken promises are fuelling young people's anger
content: France, Belgium, Spain, Albania – young people have taken to the streets across Europe in recent weeks. Their grievances are different – school conditions, housing, or corrupt governments. Many of these protests reflect a shared frustration: the feeling that Europe's politics is failing to deliver for the next generation. A 2026 survey showed that just over half of 16- to 26-year-olds in Europe are optimistic about their future, down from 70% in 2017. First broken promise: education In France, the ongoing student protests were sparked by poor school conditions, teacher shortages, and overcrowded classrooms. It's a common problem across European countries: in Germany, municipalities report a €68.9 billion backlog in school building repairs. In the Netherlands' five biggest cities, more than one in eight primary-school teaching posts are vacant. In Italy, one in three school buildings needs urgent repairs. title: A year of fruits
content: We recently published a story asking what eating seasonally even means. Fruit likes to make that question even trickier. Some apples can lounge in storage for months, while pears are picked firm and left to soften at home. So an apple in March might be less of a “spring fruit” than autumn’s very long goodbye. Strawberries get up to their own calendar mischief. Some varieties deliver one big summer rush, and others keep fruiting for much longer. Strawberry season, it turns out, can have an encore.

title: EU governments are sweating over trade with China
content: For years, China has been selling far more to EU customers than it buys in return. The EU imported nearly €54 billion worth of goods in July, while exporting only €17.4 billion. That's a difference of €36.5 billion, or more than €1 billion a day flowing from EU countries to China. Over the past decade, that deficit has more than doubled in value as the EU keeps buying more from China, increasingly higher-value goods. European manufacturers and retailers complain that they can no longer compete with Chinese rivals who sell their products for far less, partly thanks to government subsidies that help cover their costs. Lower exports and sales of EU goods hurt the EU economy and can put EU companies out of business. This kind of trade imbalance “is unsustainable,” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said in a speech last month. “It shows in our communities and in factories across our Union. It leads to deindustrialisation in the industrial heartlands of Europe.” Last week, EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič asked China nicely to stop selling so much and to make it easier for Europeans to sell to Chinese customers. title: “Throw us some teachers, not tear gas”
content: Dinosaurs, unicorns, and Spidermen are still protesting on French streets, alongside live brass bands, teachers having “aura battles” with their students, and signs that read “throw us some teachers, not tear gas” or “I wish I was as hot as my classroom”. The ongoing student protests and school blockades are entering their fourth week, with 480,000 students taking to the streets yesterday (13 October). “We’ve invented this mobile blockade concept,” 15-year-old Ethan told us, at a protest in the city of Angers. “We have a trolley and we’ve decorated it, we have some fun banners, a French flag, and a yellow vest!” That’s a nod to the 2018 Yellow Vest protests. While it's a nationwide movement now, that has already inspired other protests abroad, like in Belgium, the student protests started in two banlieues (French suburbs): Créteil, in Val-de-Marne to the south of Paris, and Saint-Denis to the north, before spreading to other banlieues and later to schools across France. Often associated with poverty and crime, the banlieues have long been a point of contention in French politics, but also in French society as a whole. title: How to (maybe) turn off Russian bots
content: Over four days last week, Ukrainian drones hit data centres run by Yandex, known as “Russia's Google”. Soon after, claims spread that bot traffic online had gone down. While anecdotally true, it's not the full picture. Let's dive in. Ukraine struck three main sites. One of the largest reportedly housed two of Yandex's three supercomputers. Banks, retailers, mobile operators, and news sites across Russia suffered outages, and automated web traffic from Yandex's network fell to near zero, according to Cloudflare. Many users on social media then said they noticed a drop in Russian bot activity online. “When Ukraine destroys Russian data centres, hordes of aggressive right-wing bots disappear, and Twitter becomes much friendlier. Isn’t that interesting?” wrote historian Timothy Snyder on X. “The far right should declare three days of mourning,” wrote Radosław Sikorski, Poland's foreign minister, on X (and later deleted). Many of Russia's online services run on Yandex’s cloud infrastructure so it's plausible all activity, including bot traffic, would be impacted by an outage.
